newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Frontrunner demands sovereignty as Chechens vote.
newsitem.headline: Frontrunner demands sovereignty as Chechens vote.

text.p: The guerrilla leader who is widely expected to win Chechnya's presidential election vowed on Sunday to turn Russia's breakaway Moslem region into an internationally-recognised sovereign state.
Aslan Maskhadov, speaking on the eve of the election, also said that as Chechen president he would demand "war reparations" from Russia to compensate for the devastation of the region.

He dismissed fears of an "Afghan or Tajik scenario", of civil war as a product of the rhetoric of hardline rivals such as Shamil Basayev. A victory by Basayev, who rose to fame after leading a bloody raid on the south Russian town of Budennovsk, could fulfil Moscow's worst nightmares.

Maskhadov, who hopes to win the peace as convincingly as he defeated Russia's troops in 21 months of war, said it seemed Moscow was in no mood to negotiate on giving Chechnya's de facto independence more legal substance.

"The whole world, including Russia, will have to recognise that the elections are democratic and to recognise the legitimate authority of this popularly elected president and sit down at the negotiating table right away," he told reporters.
"We want to be recognised as a sovereign state."
In Moscow, a deputy foreign minister underlined Kremlin sensitivity over the issue of sovereignty.
Viktor Posuvalyuk said Russia was ready to break off relations with any country which granted Chechnya diplomatic recognition.
"We have warned the entire international community," he said, but acknowledged there were no signs yet of any country making a move to do so.
President Boris Yeltsin sent troops into Chechnya in 1994 to prevent it seceding. Maskhadov's fighters humiliated them.
But Moscow, worried about security and fearing a spread of separatism to other ethnic groups, still wants to stop the small but sensitive frontier region from breaking away.

For Yeltsin, recovering on Sunday from heart surgery and a recent bout of pneumonia, the mere holding of the elections constitutes a defeat. The president himself has described the Chechen campaign as a blunder.
But few countries would entertain the notion of sacrificing relations with Russia in order to grant recognition to a region with a prewar population of one million people.
Speaking at his farmhouse headquarters outside Grozny, the 45-year-old former Soviet colonel, sporting a traditional lambswool cap, said he was confident of beating his 15 rivals.

Maskhakov's popularity is due as much to his leading role in the peace talks with Moscow that culminated in these elections as to his leadership during the war, which ended with his audacious seizure of the Chechen capital last August.
More than 100 outside observers, including Russians, were in the north Caucasus region to see the vote is fair.

Maskhadov said he believed Russian special forces might try to disrupt the election. For that reason he hoped to secure the 50 percent of the vote needed on Monday to avoid dragging it out to a run-off in two weeks.
The Chechen authorities have laid on elaborate security for foreign observers and journalists.

The chief European mediator in Chechnya, Swiss diplomat Tim Guldimann, told Reuters the 75 monitors from the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe would have armed Chechen escorts, helicopter cover and be in constant radio contact.
"I don't see any problems with these elections from the security point of view," he said. OSCE officials have helped fund the running of the poll and say they are satisfied so far.

Chechnya is awash with guns, however, and the increasingly bellicose rhetoric of the election campaign has kindled fears that it could descend into factional fighting among armed groups loyal to the different guerrilla leaders running for president.
Maskhadov's first priority if he won would be to bring order to Chechnya's armed groups and control their weapons.

Basayev is popular among the young and espouses a more fervent brand of Islamic rule than Maskhadov. He could force a run-off, as could Zelimkhan Yandarbiyev, who became the rebels' leader when the charismatic Dzhokhar Dudayev was killed last April. Rebel spokesman Movladi Udugov also has solid support.

In their first ever internationally monitored elections, Chechens will also choose from among some 850 candidates standing for 63 seats in a new regional assembly. Results are expected to start coming in on Tuesday.
